name: Lachixío Zapotec
confidence_why: Sicoli's 2007 dissertation, as summarized by Bueno Holle 2019, puts the single primary stress on the root of a [[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic] word with a trochaic foot, and Sicoli 1999 is consistent with this (native stress predictable and non-final, the stressed syllable preceding the medial consonant in CVCV native words, Spanish loans assimilated to penultimate stress), with no source disagreeing; the account rests on one fieldworker, and the deciding statement is second-hand, since Sicoli 1999 never spells the rule out.

catalog_quote: [Sicoli 1999: 396] Stress on some loanwords may not follow from otherwise predictable rules. ... Example (3) shows the preservation of a liquid-obstruent sequence, a syllable (and word) final nasal, and final syllable stress. All of these features violate the system of phonological constraints that were operational in the precontact Lachixío phonological system. (3) kolcho!n [kolˈtʃóŋ] <b-- [kolˈtʃoŋ] 'colchón // mattress' [p. 399] positions within the phonological word. In native words, only voiceless obstruents are permitted medially (after a stressed syllable) and only voiceless obstruents are permitted word-initially in monosyllables: CVTV and TV (*CVDV, *DV), where <T> represents any voiceless obstruent and <D> any voiced obstruent. [Table (9): (b) béxo [ˈvéʃ:ó] 'peso // meausre' [sic]; (c) xombólo [ʃoˈmból:ó] 'sombrero // hat'; (f) sonája [soˈnáx:á] 'sonaja // rattle'] [Bueno Holle 2019: 19, reporting Sicoli 2007] He describes Lachixío Zapotec as a "stress-timed" language where there is only primary (no secondary) stress which is non-iterative, that is, has at most one stress foot. ... The maximal phonological word is composed of a clitic phrase with the following structure: [[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic]. The metrical foot, the unit counted for rhythm, is trochaic.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word, on the lexical root: native words are CV́TV or TV́ with the stressed syllable preceding the medial (voiceless, often geminate) obstruent, i.e. a trochaic foot on the root; proclitics and enclitics are unstressed ([[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic] per Bueno Holle 2019: 18 reporting Sicoli 2007). Word-final stress is foreign to the native system and survives only in unassimilated Spanish loans. In a bare disyllabic root this is penultimate stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sicoli 1999 is silent. Bueno Holle 2019: 18, reporting Sicoli 2007: 'only primary (no secondary) stress which is non-iterative, that is, has at most one stress foot'.
new_statements.exceptions: Unassimilated Spanish loans may keep final-syllable stress (kolcho!n [kolˈtʃoŋ] 'mattress', jardin [xarˈdin] 'garden'); 'Stress on some loanwords may not follow from otherwise predictable rules' (p. 396). Assimilated loans take the native pattern (kalo [ˈkal:o] 'broth', sonaja [soˈnax:a] 'rattle').
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root plus clitics); the 1999 examples are isolated citation forms in a practical orthography with an acute accent marking stress and IPA with ˈ. The statement is indirect: Sicoli states that native words have a stressed syllable before the medial obstruent (CVTV) and that final stress violates native constraints; he never writes a one-line stress rule. Phrase-level emphasis (gemination/lengthening of the stressed foot) and boundary tones are described in Sicoli 2007 per Bueno Holle 2019: 18.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Zapotec of Santa María Lachixío (Sola de Vega district, Oaxaca), which Sicoli 1999: 395 calls 'a dialect of the Solteco branch'; this is Glottolog lach1249 / ISO zpl (also listed under Zimatlán/Western Zapotec names). Sicoli 2007 additionally covers Asunción Mixtepec Zapotec (zoo, asun1236); the Bueno Holle 2019 report concerns Lachixío only.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record has an empty rule; the existing_statement is this same paper (same p. 396 quote) but labelled 'morphologically determined', which the text does not support: Sicoli says native stress is rule-predictable and non-final and says nothing about morphological conditioning. The 1999 evidence is compatible with the second-hand report of Sicoli 2007 in Bueno Holle 2019 (one primary stress per phonological word on the root, trochaic foot, no secondary stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in native Lachixío words follows predictable rules and is not word-final: final-syllable stress (as in the unassimilated loan kolchón 'mattress', p. 396) is one of the features that violate the precontact system, while the assimilated loan kalo ['kal:o] < caldo (p. 395) carries stress on the first syllable, and native disyllables are described as CVTV with the medial obstruent 'after a stressed syllable', i.e. stress on the first (penultimate) syllable of a CVCV word. The paper never states the rule outright; 'penultimate/root-initial, non-final, predictable' is an inference from these three passages.
new_statements.exceptions: Unassimilated Spanish loanwords may keep final-syllable stress and other foreign features (p. 396); stress on such loans 'may not follow from otherwise predictable rules'.
new_statements.identity_note: Persons 1997 describes Santa María Lachixío (district of Sola de Vega, Oaxaca) and names San Vicente Lachixío and San Miguel Mixtepec as closely related varieties (about 85% intelligibility); Sicoli 1999 writes simply 'Lachixío' (his field site is Santa María Lachixío in the 2007/2010 work). Nothing opened describes a different variety.

new_statements.relation_note: Silent on placement, so it neither confirms nor disputes the catalog's morphological coding; it adds first-hand (1974-78 fieldwork) confirmation that Lachixío has word stress alongside four tones and that the stress correlate is post-tonic consonant lengthening, the same cue Sicoli 1999 (p. 399, CVTV) and Sicoli 2016 (heavy trochee) describe.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A discourse paper; its only phonological statement is endnote 2: four contrastive tones (1 high.. 4 low, with glides), vowels plain/long/checked/interrupted, and word stress presupposed (voiceless stops, nasals, lateral and semivowels geminate intervocalically after the stressed syllable). It does not say where stress falls. The whole chapter (pp. 123-140) and the volume introduction were scanned-read: no other occurrence of stress/accent; 'tone' recurs only for the stative vs unreal aspect contrast (p. 126) and the imperative (note 4).
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe the Zapotec of Santa María Lachixío, Sola de Vega district, Oaxaca (ISO zpl): the 2009 grammar 'registra el habla de la población de Santa María Lachixío' and names dialect variants in San Vicente Lachixío and San Miguel Mixtepec; Persons 1979's texts are from Santa María Lachixío speakers recorded 1974-78; Sicoli 2016's corpus was recorded in Santa María Lachixío in 2008-2009.

new_statements.quote: Como en español, el zapoteco tiene contraste entre palabras por la posición de la sílaba tónica. Las mismas reglas que rigen la representación ortográfica del acento en español son válidas para las palabras del zapoteco. Por eso, como la gran mayoría de ellas tienen acento en la penúltima sílaba y terminan en vocal, no escribimos acento ortográfico. No se escribe el acento ortográfico sobre las vocales quebradas porque siempre forman una sílaba tónica. Las monosílabas llevan acento ortográfico únicamente cuando éste es necesario para la distinción de dos palabras que, de otra manera, parecerían iguales.
new_statements.translation: As in Spanish, Zapotec has contrast between words by the position of the stressed syllable. The same rules that govern the orthographic representation of the accent in Spanish are valid for Zapotec words. Therefore, since the great majority of them are stressed on the penultimate syllable and end in a vowel, we write no orthographic accent. No orthographic accent is written on broken vowels [VꞌV] because they always form a stressed syllable. Monosyllables carry an orthographic accent only when it is needed to distinguish two words that would otherwise look the same.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the on-file statement 'fixed: penultimate syllable' (Sicoli 1999) in that penultimate stress is the majority pattern, and with the catalog's 'morphological' coding in that word-level position is not fixed; it ADDS that position is contrastive between words, that VꞌV vowels are always tonic, and the four-tone inventory. The two are reconcilable if the non-penult words are prefixed monosyllabic roots, clit…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress exists alongside a four-tone system (every syllable bears a tone: rising, high, mid, low; tones written 1-4 only where needed). Stress position is contrastive between words, as in Spanish; the great majority of words are stressed on the penultimate syllable and end in a vowel, so stress is left unmarked there and Spanish accent-mark rules flag the others; 'broken' (interrupted, VꞌV) vowels are always in the stressed syllable; monosyllables get an accent mark only to disambiguate (and í additionally marks high tone, p. 2). In effect: penultimate default with lexically marked exceptions; the grammar gives no morphological conditioning and no further stress rule anywhere else (searched acento/acentua/tónica/sílaba/énfasis through all 112 pp; other hits concern tone or the í tone mark). Final-stressed Zapotec forms written with an acute do occur in the examples (e.g. xilá, nelá/neelá, liꞌá, riꞌá, itá).
new_statements.exceptions: a minority of words are not penultimate-stressed (written with the Spanish orthographic accent); broken vowels VꞌV always stressed; monosyllables

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the on-file 'fixed: penultimate syllable' statement and with Sicoli 1999 p. 399 (native template CVTV with the obstruent 'after a stressed syllable') and adds the mechanism: a durational heavy-trochee template (post-tonic gemination or tonic-vowel lengthening) plus a bimoraic minimal word; compatible with the catalog's morphological (root/stem-based) coding since the template is stated over the minimal word/stem and tone is said to spread 'to the end of the stem'. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Brief but explicit (a transcription-conventions section, the only place stress is treated; body searched for stress/accent/tone/prosod/syllab): Lachixío words obey a bimoraic minimal word ((C)VV monosyllables) and disyllables are heavy trochees (C)VX.CV, i.e. stress on the first = penultimate syllable of a disyllable, with the weight slot X filled by geminating the post-tonic consonant (if voiceless or sonorant) or lengthening the tonic vowel (if the post-tonic consonant is voiced); long segments are therefore predictable from stress, not contrastive. Tone (high/low/contours) is marked independently. No statement for longer words or clitic groups; the author refers to Sicoli 2007 for the full account of stress, word and syllable structure.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned here (Bueno Holle 2019: 18, held in the same folder, reports Sicoli 2007 as saying there is only primary, non-iterative stress, one trochaic foot per word)
new_statements.exceptions: none; Spanish loans noted only for the /q/ spelling
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe the Zapotec of Santa María Lachixío, Sola de Vega district, Oaxaca (ISO zpl): the 2009 grammar 'registra el habla de la población de Santa María Lachixío' and names dialect variants in San Vicente Lachixío and San Miguel Mixtepec; Persons 1979's texts are from Santa María Lachixío speakers recorded 1974-78; Sicoli 2016's corpus was recorded in Santa María Lachixío in 2008-2009.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the sources themselves. Sicoli 1999 (first-hand): native stress is predictable and non-final, first syllable of CVCV native words stressed, Spanish loans may keep final stress. Bueno Holle 2019 (held by the project, second-hand summary of Sicoli 2007 pp. 18-19): Lachixío has 'only primary (no secondary) stress which is non-iterative', a trochaic foot, and a maximal phonological word [[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic]. Sicoli 2010 (held by the project) adds phonemic low tone (imperative marked by L) and says nothing about stress placement; Persons 1997 describes a high-pitch respect register only. The one conflict is with the catalog's own label: the existing statement tags Sicoli 1999 as 'morphologically determined', a reading the text does not contain. No hard contradiction, but one difference of framing to settle. The specialist sources (Sicoli 1999 p. 399 native template CVTV; Sicoli 2016 p. 207 heavy trochees in disyllables with post-tonic gemination, tone spreading to the end of the stem; Sicoli 2007 as reported by Bueno Holle 2019 p. 18: one non-iterative trochaic stress foot on the root inside [[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic]) support the catalog's root-based ('morphological') coding, which surfaces as penultimate stress in the typical disyllabic word. Las monosílabas llevan acento ortográfico únicamente cuando éste es necesario para la distinción de dos palabras que, de otra manera, parecerían iguales.
